title.en: Ori, the God of Fate in Every House
title.zh: 奧里——家家供奉的命運之神

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the household coffer near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊家宅藏櫃）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. III

summary.en: The Ori (head) is the universal household deity, worshipped by both sexes as the god of fate: good or ill fortune attends one according to the will or decree of this god, and it is propitiated that good luck might be the votary's share. The representing image is forty-one cowries strung together in the shape of a crown, secreted in a large coffer, the lid of which is of the same form and material — called Ile Ori, Ori's house, and as large as the owner can afford to make it; some contain as much as six heads of cowries, and the leather-worker who makes it is paid the same number of cowries as he uses. As the Kori is the children's god, so the Ori is exclusively worshipped by adults; after the death of its owner the image with the coffer is destroyed, and the cowries spent.
summary.zh: 「奧里」（頭）是普受男女供奉的家宅之神——命運之神：禍福皆繫於祂的旨意，故人人奉祭以求好運。其神像為四十一枚貝幣串成王冠之形，藏於大木櫃中；櫃蓋同形同質，名「伊萊奧里」——奧里之宅，大小視主人財力而定，有的竟可容六「頭」（一萬二千枚）貝幣；製櫃的皮匠所得工錢，恰與用去的貝數相等。柯里是小兒之神，奧里則唯成人敬奉；主人亡故之後，神像與櫃同毀，貝幣隨之散盡。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921 by Johnson (an insider-adjacent Yoruba pastor-historian); the Ori (personal head-fate) cult. Cross-ref: yoruba-three-indwelling-spirits (Ellis's Olori head-spirit) and Dennett's odu readings.

passages.text: The Ori (head) is the universal household deity worshipped by both sexes as the god of fate. It is believed that good or ill fortune attends one, according to the will or decree of this god; and hence it is propitiated in order that good luck might be the share of its votary. The representing image is 41 cowries strung together in the shape of a crown. This is secreted in a large coffer, the lid of which is of the same form and material. It is called Ile Ori (Ori's house), and in size is as large as the owner can afford to make it; some usually contain as much as 6 heads (12,000) of cowries, and the manufacturer, who is generally a worker in leather, receives as his pay the same amount of cowries as is used in the article manufactured. As the Kori is the children's god, so the Ori is exclusively worshipped by the adults. After the death of its owner, the image of Ori with the coffer is destroyed, and the cowries spent.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. III (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: As the Aremo Reigned With His Father, He Must Die With Him
title.zh: 儲君與父同治，亦必與父同死

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the Aremo's residence beside the palace)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（王宮旁的儲君官邸）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. IV

summary.en: In the earliest days the eldest son succeeded his father, and to be educated in all the duties of the kingship he was associated with the father in important duties, practically reigning with him under the title of Aremo, the heir apparent, with his own official residence near the palace. But as the age grew corrupt, the Aremo often exercised sway quite as much as or more than the King himself, especially in the course of a long reign when age had rendered the monarch feeble; they had equal powers of life and death over the King's subjects, and there are cases on record of the Aremo being strongly suspected of terminating the father's life in order to attain full powers at once. It was therefore made a law and part of the constitution that as the Aremo reigned with his father, he must also die with him. This law had the effect, at any rate, of checking parricide; it continued to take effect up to last century, when (in 1858) it was repealed by Atiba, one of the later kings, in favour of his Aremo Adelu. The Aremo may now succeed if found worthy, but he must be elected in the usual way; and if passed over he must retire into private life in the provinces — unless he chooses of his own accord to die with the father.
summary.zh: 太古之制，長子承父業；為使他通曉為王之道，常使協理要務，事實上與父共治，稱「阿雷莫」——儲君，在王宮旁另設官邸。然而世風日壞，阿雷莫的權勢往往不遜於王，尤其老王年邁力衰、在位日久之時；二人生殺之權相等，史冊且載有儲君疑為早日攬權而弒父之案。於是憲制定規：儲君與父共治，亦必與父同死。此律至少遏制了弒父之行；施行至上世紀——1858年阿提巴王為其儲君阿德盧而廢之。今日儲君如經選立合格可繼位，但須循正途；若遭擯斥，便須退居外省——除非他自願隨父而死。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the companion-death constitutional law of the Oyo crown, reported with Johnson's own historical note on its 1858 repeal.

passages.text: In the earliest days, the eldest son naturally succeeded the father, and in order to be educated in all the duties of the kingship which must one day devolve upon him, he was often associated more or less with the father in performing important duties, and thereby he often performed royal functions, and thus gradually he practically reigned with his father under the title of Aremo (the heir apparent) having his own official residence near the palace. But as the age grew corrupt, the Aremo often exercised sway quite as much as or more than the King himself, especially in the course of a long reign, when age has rendered the monarch feeble. They had equal powers of life and death over the King's subjects, and there are some cases on record of the Aremo being strongly suspected of terminating the father's life, in order to attain full powers at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV (1921); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was therefore made a law and part of the constitution that as the Aremo reigned with his father, he must also die with him. This law had the effect, at any rate, of checking parricide. It continued to take effect up to last century when (in 1858) it was repealed by Atiba, one of the later Kings, in favour of his Aremo Adelu. The Aremo may now succeed if found worthy, but he must be elected in the usual way; but if passed over or rejected by the king-makers he must leave the city and resort to a private retirement in the provinces. This, however, is not really obligatory, but as he must be superseded in his office, such a course is inevitable, unless he chooses of his own accord to die with the father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV (1921); not verbatim.

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the Otun-Iwefa's house where the king-elect is fed)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（王儲受饗的奧圖-伊韋法宅邸）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. IV, note

summary.en: Tradition says that in the early times, while the King-elect is in the Otun-Iwefa's house, among other dishes brought to him to partake of is one prepared from the heart of the late King, which has been extracted and preserved. After partaking of this, he is told he has eaten the King: hence the origin of the word Je Oba — to become a King, literally to eat a King.
summary.zh: 相傳古時王儲居於奧圖-伊韋法宅邸期間，奉到他面前與諸餚並陳的，有一道取自已故先王心臟烹製的菜——那心臟已被取出保存。食畢，有人告訴他：「你已食王。」——「傑奧巴」（Je Oba，登基為王）一詞由此而來，字面義即「食王」。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921 as Johnson's footnote on the coronation sequence; the king-continuity rite reported as the recorded tradition states it, without graphic elaboration.

passages.text: Tradition says that in the early times while the King-elect is in the Otun-Iwefa's house, among other dishes brought to him to partake of is one prepared from the heart of the late King which has been extracted and preserved. After partaking of this he is told he has eaten the King. Hence the origin of the word Je Oba, to become a King (lit. to eat a King).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV, note (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: The Bara: The Mausoleum a King Enters Once
title.zh: 巴拉陵——君王一生僅入一次

region.en: Oyo, Nigeria (the royal mausoleum on the city's outskirts)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧約城（城郊的王家陵廟）

source.work: Rev. Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (London, 1921), Part I ch. IV

summary.en: The coronation takes place at the end of three months, really at the third appearance of the new moon after the late King's death, and is attended with great public demonstration. This day is generally known as the King's visit to the Bara. The Bara or royal mausoleum is a consecrated building in the outskirts of the city, under the care of a high-priestess named Iyamode; there the Kings were formally crowned, and there buried. The King enters it but once in his lifetime, and that is on the day of his coronation.
summary.zh: 加冕禮於三個月之期滿時舉行——實即先王崩後第三次新月出現之時，全城盛裝慶賀，四方來賀者雲集。此日通稱「王臨巴拉」。巴拉即王家陵廟，是城郊一座奉為聖地的建築，由名為「伊亞莫德」的女大祭司執掌；歷代君王皆在此正式加冕，亦皆歸葬於此。而國王一生只入此門一次——就在他加冕的那一天。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1921; the Bara rite binding coronation to the tomb. Cross-ref: yoruba-ida-oranyan-coronation (the Ife sword requirement).

passages.text: The coronation takes place at the end of three months, really at the third appearance of the new moon after the late King's death. The date is generally so fixed as to have it, if possible, before the next great festival. It is attended with a great public demonstration. It is a gala day in which the whole city appears in holiday dress. Visitors from the provinces and representatives of neighbouring states also flock into the city in numbers. This day is generally known as the King's visit to the Bara. The Bara or royal mausoleum is a consecrated building in the outskirts of the city, under the care of a high-priestess named Iyamode; there the Kings were formally crowned, and there buried. The King enters it but once in his lifetime, and that is on the day of his coronation.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, The History of the Yorubas, Part I ch. IV (1921); not verbatim.

title.en: Ogun Turns the Smith's Tools to Stone: The Anvil of Lade
title.zh: 奧貢化鐵為石——鐵匠拉德的鐵砧

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the Oni's monument square, where the anvil stands)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（奧尼宮前聖物園中的鐵砧）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: In the Oni's palace at Ife, within a small space surrounded by a low wall, there is a ring of holy stones — and the strangest is an onion or drop-shaped block thirty inches in height and forty-one and a half inches round, which, though it is of iron, the people in general say is stone. The story of it is this: this stone was the anvil of Lade, the smith. Lade was the mightiest smith of the past; when he died, Ogun changed all his tools into stone. The stone in the Oni's palace is Lade's anvil, and its name is Ogun-Lade. It was washed out of the earth in a season of rains at the exact time when the Koran was brought into the land — so the legend. The material cracks off in cup-shaped scales, and a second like it, obviously sacrosanct, was found in the most secret parts of the Oni's palace, judged by its exterior to be cast and not wrought.
summary.zh: 伊費奧尼宮內，低牆環繞的小園中供著一圈聖石——最奇者是一塊洋蔥（或水滴）形巨物，高三十吋、周長四十一吋半；它雖是鐵鑄，人們卻堅稱是石。傳說如此：此石本是鐵匠拉德的鐵砧。拉德是古昔最偉大的鐵匠；他一死，奧貢便把他所有的工具都化成了石頭。奧尼宮中此石即拉德之砧，名為「奧貢-拉德」。相傳它是某個雨季從土中沖刷而出——恰在《可蘭經》傳入本地之時。其質地層層剝落如杯狀鱗片；在奧尼宮最深秘處另有一件同類聖物，觀其外表應為鑄造而非鍛打。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the petrified-tools legend of the smith Lade tied to Ogun's patronage of smiths. Johnson's Koran-contact tradition (yoruba-odudua-koran-peg) is echoed in the dating formula.

passages.text: Still stranger, however, is the monument placed between the two above-mentioned ones in the same place, namely, an onion or drop-shaped block thirty inches in height and forty-one and a half inches round, and thus a large and important specimen, when one remembers it is of iron! Although it is metal, the people in general say it is stone. The story of it is this: this stone was the anvil of Lade, the smith. Lade was the mightiest smith of the past. When he died, Ogun changed all his tools into stone. The stone in the Oni's palace is Lade's anvil, and its name is Ogun-Lade. It was washed out of the earth in a season of rains at the exact time when the Koran was brought into the land. So the legend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: The material of this lump cracks off in cup-shaped scales. The shape of the thing did not allow me to see whether this, considered from the point of view of African technical ability, was a gigantic piece of wrought iron or, as is less likely, a block of cast-iron. Later on, in the most secret parts of the Oni's palace, Martius came upon another like it, obviously sacrosanct, and his engineering knowledge led him to conclude that, judging by its exterior, it was cast and not wrought.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: The Sixteen-Part Shadow Clock of Ife

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the triangular monolith in the centre of the old town)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（古城中央的三角巨石）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: The real type of the tooth-stone monoliths is found frequently both in Ife and in ruined Modeke; they stand upright on slight elevations. One of these triangular monoliths, nearly eleven feet nine inches high, stands in the centre of the old town: the natives said it had formerly served as a kind of sundial. When the shadow of this stele reached a point on a circle drawn round it, it was time for certain sacred festivals — and this circle was divided into sixteen parts, which caused no surprise, for this number constantly recurs everywhere. These monoliths, then, were essentially time-measurers and sun-clocks.
summary.zh: 「齒石」類獨石柱在伊費與已毀的莫達凱凱屢見不鮮，皆立於微微隆起的高地。古城中央一座三角獨石柱高近十一呎九吋：土人相傳它古時用作日晷。當柱影觸及環繞柱基所畫圓周上的某點，便是舉行特定聖祭之期——而那圓周被分成十六等分，此數無處不現，不足為奇。這些獨石柱，本質上是量時之器、太陽之鐘。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the sixteen-part festival calendar stone, tying Ife's sacred geography to the Ifa sixteen (Frobenius's analysis). Cross-ref: yoruba-four-gods-four-quarters.

passages.text: The height of Oranja's obelisk above the ground was close upon eleven feet, nine inches. If, now, the Oranja tooth-stone takes on the monolith form, we find the real type of this frequently both in Ife and also in ruined Modeke. They stand upright on slight elevations. One of these triangular monoliths is illustrated on page 299. The natives said it had formerly served as a kind of sundial. When the shadow of this stele reached a point on a circle drawn round it, it was time for certain sacred festivals. This circle was divided into sixteen parts, which caused us no surprise, for this number constantly recurs everywhere. These monoliths, then, were essentially time-measurers and sun-clocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Illu-Olokun: The Town Where All Mankind Was Born
title.zh: 伊盧奧洛貢——全人類誕生之城

region.en: Igbo-Olokun forest, north of Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the drowned city's site)
region.zh: 伊費以北的伊格博-奧洛貢森林（沈沒古城之址）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: There once was an old town called Illu-Olokun, the Town of the Ruler of the Ocean, to the north of Ife. Our fathers before us have told us that in times long, long ago this city was surrounded by a lake to the south and a river on the north, by which one could get to the sea. Olokun, the Orisha, had founded this city before the creation of the earth; the Omo-Olokun, long since driven to the south, left behind them the tradition that it actually was Olokun who created the earth on which Ife stood. In former days he was the only god worshipped in Illu-Olokun and in Ife. The legendary name of the Sea God, Isindya's first priest, and of the first king, was Oba-Idyo. Illu-Olokun was believed to be the birthplace of all mankind, both fair and dark — the Europeans also came from there! The place where once it stood is to-day called Igbo-Olokun, because a great forest has overgrown it; but the name Ebolokun, sacrifice to the Sea God, is commoner, because offerings are still laid before the Poseidon of Atlantic Africa under the palms in the forest. In the depths of this vast forest there are large jars of glazed porcelain, and the discovery of Ebolokun furnishes proof that at some remote era glass was made and moulded in this very land — the beautiful long glass beads said to be found only in the temple of Olokun.
summary.zh: 伊費之北曾有古城，名「伊盧奧洛貢」——海王之城。祖輩相傳：太古之時，此城南湖北河環繞，循水道可通大海。海神奧洛貢在大地被造之前便建立了此城；早已南遷的奧莫-奧洛貢族人留下遺訓：伊費所立的大地，正是奧洛貢所造。古時伊盧奧洛貢與伊費所拜的唯一神祇便是祂。海神之號、伊斯因迪亞的首位祭司兼開國君王，傳說名為奧巴-伊迪約。伊盧奧洛貢被奉為全人類——膚白膚黑皆是——的誕生之地，連歐洲人也出自那裡！古城舊址今日稱「伊格博-奧洛貢」，因參天密林已將其吞沒；但更通行的名字是「埃博洛貢」——祭獻海神——因為人們至今仍在大西洋非洲的這位「波塞冬」面前的棕櫚林中擺放祭品。茫茫林海深處藏著大件釉瓷巨罐；埃博洛貢的發現證明：遠古之世，玻璃便在此地燒製成型——那種據說只在奧洛貢神廟中才見得到的美麗長形玻璃珠。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the drowned-city legend of Illu-Olokun and the Olokun-first-creation tradition, with the glassworking archaeology Frobenius connected to it. Cross-refs: yoruba-oduduwa-sand-hen, yoruba-olokun-flood-chained.

passages.text: There once was an old town called Illu-Olokun, that is, the Town of the Ruler of the Ocean, to the north of Ilife. Our fathers before us have told us that in times long, long ago this city was surrounded by a lake to the South and a river on the North, by which one could get to the sea. Olokun, the Orisha, had founded this city before the creation of the earth. The Omo-Olokun, who long since then had been driven to the South, left behind them the tradition that it actually was Olokun who created the earth on which Ilife stood. In former days he was the only god worshipped in Illu-Olokun and in Ilife. The legendary name of the Sea God, Isindya's first priest, and of the first king, was Oba-Idyo. Illu-Olokun was believed to be the birthplace of all mankind, both fair and dark; the Europeans also came from there!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: As stated, the old city was known as Illu-Olokun. The place where once it stood is to-day called Igbo-Olokun, because a great Igbo, or forest, has overgrown it. But the name Ebolokun, or Ebo-olokun, i.e. sacrifice to the Sea God, is commoner, because offerings are still laid before the Poseidon of Atlantic Africa under the palms in the forest. In the depths of this vast forest there are large jars of glazed porcelain; and the discovery of Ebolokun and the Ebora furnishes proof that at some remote era glass was made and moulded in this very land, and that the nation which here of old held rule were brilliant exponents of apt dexterity in the production of terra-cotta images.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Olokun's Holy Hill in Ilesha Country
title.zh: 伊萊沙之地的奧洛貢聖丘

region.en: Ilesha district, Nigeria (the secret tumulus of the sea god)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊萊沙近郊（海神的秘密古塚）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: The Ilifians believe that the Ocean deity lives not only in the sea, but dwells also in the beds of the streams, and the Niger itself is one of his favourite abodes. Nay, there was a myth current with the Ileshans according to which Olokun lived on a hill — and this fits in with the tale in which Shankpanna changed Olokun into a hill at Olorun's command. Frobenius declines to mention the site of Olokun's Holy Hill, about which the Ileshans fully informed him, limiting himself to saying that it is obviously an old tumulus which could be reached, within comparatively recent times, by a sacrificial path; he is told its interior is richly adorned — the natives declare that all its wall-coverings, headgear and body ornaments are of gold, though from what he could personally gather it must rather consist in the main of bronze with only small quantities of the precious metal.
summary.zh: 伊費人相信海神不只居於海中，也棲於河床——尼日河本身就是他鍾愛的居所之一。伊萊沙人中更流傳著一則神話：奧洛貢住在山上——這與香潘納奉奧洛倫之命把奧洛貢化為山丘的故事正相呼應。弗羅貝紐斯獲伊萊沙人詳告聖丘所在，卻不肯揭示其址，只說那顯然是一座古塚，直至晚近尚有一條祭祀小徑可達；據聞塚內陳設華美——土人堅稱壁飾、冠冕、佩飾盡為黃金；但據他親自考察所及，主體應為青銅，貴金屬僅佔少數。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the hill-tumulus cult of Olokun (site withheld by Frobenius and by this record). Cross-refs: yoruba-edju-four-houses-trick (Olokun changed to a hill), yoruba-oke-abeokuta-cavern.

passages.text: The Ilifians, however, believe that the Ocean deity lives not only in the sea, but rather dwells also in the beds of the streams, and the Niger itself is one of his favourite abodes. Nay, there was a myth current with the Ileshans according to which Olokun lived on a hill. But this also fits in with a tale told above, in which Shankpanna changed Olokun into a hill at Olorun's command. I do not consider it advisable here to mention the site of Olokun's Holy Hill, about which the Ileshans fully informed me. I will limit myself to saying that it is obviously an old tumulus, which could be reached within comparatively recent times by a sacrificial path. I am told its interior is richly adorned. The natives declare that all its wall-coverings, all the headgear and body ornaments, in fact, all its decorations, are of gold. But from what I was able personally to gather, I think this must be a mistake: it may even now, with almost positive certainty, be said that in the main it consists of bronze with only small quantities of the precious metal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

title.en: Three Spirits in Every Man: Head, Stomach and Great Toe
title.zh: 人人三靈——頭、胃與大足趾

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the household shrine near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊家宅神龕）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VII

summary.en: The Yorubas hold that each man has three spiritual inmates: Olori (lord of the head), sometimes called Ori, the protector, guardian and guide, who brings good fortune — offerings of fowls are made to him and the blood mixed with palm-oil rubbed on the forehead, his symbol being half a calabash studded with cowries; Ipin-ijeun, he who shares in the food, who shares in all the man eats and has no special sacrifice — hunger is personified as his agent, pinching the stomach to convey his principal's desire; and Ipori, the great toe, least important of the three, anointed with fowl's blood and palm-oil when a man is about to set out on a journey — a waterfowl, says the proverb, is not fit for the worship of Ipori. Curiously, Ipin-ijeun is connected with fire-worship: fire, which has no god of its own, is still spoken of as Abanigbele, the Inmate — for fire is necessary to prepare food, and food is necessary to Ipin-ijeun; therefore he takes fire under his protection and takes care that it is not extinguished.
summary.zh: 約魯巴人相信每個人身中住著三個靈：一是「奧洛里」（頭之主），或稱「奧里」——守護者、引導者，司掌好運；以雞祭之，血和棕櫚油抹額，其符為半邊嵌貝的葫蘆。二是「伊平-伊杰恩」——分食之靈，人吃什麼他分什麼，故無專祭；「饑餓」被擬人化為他的使者，掐胃以傳主人欲食之意。三是「伊波里」——大足趾之靈，三者中最卑微，唯臨行之際以雞血調油塗趾；諺云：水禽不配祭伊波里。奇妙的是，伊平-伊杰恩與拜火相連：約魯巴本無火神，火卻被稱為「阿巴尼格貝萊」——「同住者」——因為造食需火，而伊平-伊杰恩需食；他遂把火納入庇護之下，不許它熄滅。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1894; the triple-soul doctrine (compare the kra/luvo theories of the Tshi and Ewe). Cross-ref: yoruba-ori-head-fate (Johnson's Ori cult), yoruba-abiku-spirit-children.

passages.text: The Yorubas hold that each man has three spiritual inmates: Olori (owner, or lord, of the head), sometimes called Ori (head, faculty, talent), seems to be the spirit which answers to the kra or luvo. He is the protector, guardian, and guide. Offerings are made to him, chiefly fowls, and some of the blood, mixed with palm-oil, is rubbed upon the forehead. Olori brings good-fortune, whence the proverb: Olori causes the owner of the head to prosper, and not the crab on the bank of the river. The symbol of Olori is half a calabash studded over with cowries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ipin-ijeun, or ipin-ojeun (ipin, share, portion; ijeun, act of eating; hence he who shares in the food), is perhaps considered the most important of the three indwelling spirits, but as he shares in all that the man eats, he has no special sacrifice offered to him. A proverb says: There is no orisha like the stomach; it receives food every day. In some respects hunger (ebi) seems to be personified, and to be considered the agent of Ipin-ijeun; for he is said to communicate to the man, by pinching his stomach, the desire of his principal for food. Ipori, the great toe, is the least important of the three guardian spirits, and sacrifice is rarely offered to him except when a man is about to set out on a journey, in which case he anoints the great toe with a mixture of fowl's blood and palm-oil; a proverb says, a waterfowl is not fit for the worship of Ipori.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Curiously enough, Ipin-ijeun is connected with fire-worship. There is among the Yorubas no god of fire, but fire (ina) was probably once personified, for it is still spoken of as Abanigbele, the Inmate. The natives explain the connection between the two by saying that fire is necessary for the preparation of food, and food is necessary to Ipin-ijeun; therefore he takes fire under his protection, and takes care that it is not extinguished. A proverbial saying runs: Ipin-ijeun does not allow fire to depart from the earth. When fire could only be produced by the tedious process of rubbing together two sticks, it was no doubt important to keep one or two embers of a fire always smouldering.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: Ipo-Oku, the Land of the Dead Beneath the Earth
title.zh: 伊波-奧庫——地下的亡者之國

region.en: Yoruba under-world (symbolic pin: beneath the burial floor of a compound near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴冥界（象徵定位：伊費近郊院落葬地之下）

source.work: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (London, 1894), ch. VII

summary.en: The ghost-man, or soul, is called Iwun or Okan — the latter also means heart — or Ojiji, ghost, shade or shadow. After the death of the body the ghost-man goes to Ipo-Oku, the Land of the Dead, which is beneath the earth, and where each man does that which he has been accustomed to do and holds the same social position as he did in the world. To enable the ghost to reach this land it is essential that the prescribed funeral rites be performed over him; should they be omitted, the ghost wanders about the world, cold, hungry and homeless, and runs the risk of being seized by some of the evil spirits which roam about the earth in great numbers and cast by them into Orun-apadi, the unseen world of potsherds, an uncomfortable place like a pottery furnace, heaped up with charcoal and the debris of broken earthen pots. Funeral rites cannot be performed at the moment breath leaves the body, but as an earnest of their intention, and to prevent the evil spirits from seizing the ghost, the relations at once offer a sacrifice to propitiate them; and when the corpse is buried, a fowl called Adire-iranna, the fowl that buys the road — that is, that opens a right of way — is sacrificed.
summary.zh: 亡魂稱「伊烏恩」或「奧坎」——後者亦意為「心」——或稱「奧吉吉」，鬼影、陰影。身死之後，亡魂便往「伊波-奧庫」——地下之亡者國度；在那裡人人各行其平生所業，身位一如陽世。欲使亡魂抵達彼國，必得為他行足額的葬儀；若缺其禮，亡魂便在人間流浪，又冷又餓無家可歸，還可能被遍地的惡靈捉住，擲入「奧倫-阿帕迪」——碎陶的冥府，一處如陶窯般難受的地方，堆滿木炭與破陶碎瓦。斷氣之頃固不能行葬儀，但為表誠意、防惡靈攔魂，親屬隨即獻祭以慰之；下葬之際，必殺一隻名為「阿迪雷-伊蘭納」的雞——「買路之雞」，為亡魂開闢通行之路。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1894; the Yoruba Land-of-the-Dead geography, with the Orun-apadi potsherd hell paralleling Johnson's (yoruba-orun-apadi-potsherds). Ellis's grave-word etymology: iboji, place of the ghost.

passages.text: The ghost-man, or soul, the vehicle of individual personal existence, is called Iwun, or Okan, but the latter also means heart. Another word is Ojiji, which has the meanings of ghost, shade, or shadow. After the death of the body, the ghost-man goes to Ipo-Oku, the Land of the Dead (Ipo, place; Oku, dead), which is beneath the earth, and where each man does that which he has been accustomed to do, and holds the same social position as he did in the world. To enable the ghost to reach this land it is essential that he should have the prescribed funeral rites performed over him. Should they be omitted, the ghost wanders about the world, cold, hungry, and homeless, and he runs the risk of being seized by some of the evil spirits which roam about the earth in great numbers, and cast by them into Orun-apadi, the unseen world of potsherds, an uncomfortable place like a pottery furnace, heaped up with charcoal and the debris of broken earthen pots.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.

passages.text: Funeral rites cannot, of course, be performed at the moment that breath leaves the body, but as an earnest of their intention to perform them, and to prevent the evil spirits from seizing the ghost, the relations at once offer a sacrifice to propitiate them; and when the corpse is buried, a fowl, called Adire-iranna, the fowl that buys the road, that is, that opens a right of way, is sacrificed. The dead often return to earth, and are born again in the families to which they belonged in their former life; in fact, one might say that they always return, since every mother sends for a babalawo to tell her what ancestral ghost has animated her new-born child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Ellis, The Yoruba-speaking Peoples, ch. VII (1894); not verbatim.

title.en: The Four Days of the Week That Odudua Inspired
title.zh: 奧杜杜瓦啟示的四日之週

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the market-day round around Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費周邊的集市輪迴）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, Nigerian Studies (London, 1910), ch. VI

summary.en: Upon asking people who first gave the days of the week their names, Dennett was always told that Odudua inspired them. The four days of the Yoruba week are: Jakuta's day, looked upon as a Sunday, on which they clean their houses and rub their floors and split kola for the Orishas Shango, Yemoja, Oshun and Buruku; Obatala's day, sometimes called Orishala, on which they rub the walls and floors, fill a pot of water on the altar and give part of their food to him — the white Orishas (Ijaiyi, Iluofun, Ogiyan and the rest) are worshipped on this day, appealed to by barren women, and must not be offered palm oil or pepper; Awo, Ifa's day, on which the Ifa priests renew the chalk marks on the ground in front of the altars, and Oshun and Odu are also consulted; and Odudua's or Ogun's day — when they build, clear a farm, cut a tree or hunt they split kola to Ogun, and Ija and Oshowsi are also worshipped. Odudua representing the creation, it is quite natural that they should consider her day as first in their week; the first, the fifth, the ninth and the seventeenth days, which they look upon as the beginning of a new month, are sacred to Odudua, and are all market days.
summary.zh: 問起誰首先為一週諸日命名，人們總答：是奧杜杜瓦啟示的。約魯巴一週四日：一為賈庫塔之日——視同主日，家家清屋擦地，為尚戈、耶莫雅、奧舜與布魯庫剖柯拉果；二為奧巴塔拉之日（或稱奧里夏拉）——擦牆抹地、壇上盛水、分食於神——白衣諸神（伊賈伊伊、伊盧奧芬、奧吉揚等）於此日受拜，不孕婦女特來祈求，祭之不得用棕櫚油與胡椒；三為「阿沃」——伊法之日，伊法祭司是日為諸壇前的地畫更新白堊符記，奧舜與奧杜亦於此日求問；四為奧杜杜瓦（即奧貢）之日——建屋、墾荒、伐木、狩獵之時皆向奧貢剖果，伊賈與奧肖西亦同日受拜。奧杜杜瓦代表創造，其日居一週之首自是理所當然；每月之第一、第五、第九、第十七日——他們視為新月的開端——皆為奧杜杜瓦聖日，也都是集市之日。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910; the four-day ritual week with Odudua's creative priority. Cross-ref: yoruba-four-gods-four-quarters (Frobenius's five-day and compass analysis).

passages.text: Upon asking people the question, who first gave the days of the week their names? I have always been told that Odudua inspired them. The four days of the Yoruba week, then, are: Jakuta's day, which is looked upon as a Sunday. On this day they clean their houses, and rub their floors. Then they split Kola for the Orishas Shango, Yemoja, Oshun and Buruku. Obatala's day, sometimes called Orishala. On this day they rub the walls and floor of the houses, and fill a pot of water on the altar; and when they eat they give part of their food to him. The following white Orishas are worshipped on this day: Ijaiyi, Iluofun, Ijemoiwi, Ogiyan, Alajugun, Owa Olufon. These white Orishas are appealed to by barren women, and they must not be offered palm oil or pepper.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VI (1910); not verbatim.

passages.text: Awo, or Ifa's day. The people cannot consult Ifa except through a priest; in this way he is consulted about everything. On this day the Ifa priests renew the chalk marks on the ground in front of the altars; Oshun and Odu are also consulted on this day. Odudua's or Ogun's day: when they build, or clear a farm, or cut a tree, or hunt, they split kola to Ogun. Ija and Oshowsi are also worshipped on this day. Odudua representing the creation, it is quite natural that they should consider her day as first in their week. The first, the fifth, the ninth and seventeenth days, which they look upon as the beginning of a new month, are sacred to Odudua, and are all market days.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, Nigerian Studies, ch. VI (1910); not verbatim.

title.en: Idena's Staff and the Quartz Crocodiles
title.zh: 伊德納之杖與石英鱷像

region.en: Ile-Ife, Nigeria (the Idena square and its enclosures)
region.zh: 奈及利亞伊費城（伊德納廣場及周邊聖區）

source.work: Leo Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I (London, 1913), ch. XIV

summary.en: On the Idena square of Ife stand waist-high stone pillars, roughly hewn and absolutely bare of detail; nearby, amid the weeds and fallen thatch, rises a stone image thirty-two inches high with a chain round its neck and an apron skirt, and behind it the first of the stone-stools and a dish made out of quartz — a four-square block chiselled hollow above, standing on a raised ring, and ornamented at the side with lizards: these ancient stone saucers show indications of originally being basket-work developed in wood-carving and transferred finally to sculpture in stone. In the next enclosure stands the granite statue of the Idena himself, thirty-six inches high, thick-lipped and broad-nosed, with a tassel of hair hanging from its left ear — its hair represented by little iron pegs inserted in small holes, the first instance of this singular use of iron. Before the Idena's tooth-stone or obelisk lie the pieces of a long stone slab, broken in four, which the natives call the broken buckler of the Idena; and in the last enclosure a stone crocodile stands to right and left in front of drop-stones — crocodiles of quartz, one of them still worshipped in a private compound.
summary.zh: 伊費的伊德納廣場上立著齊腰高的粗石柱，鑿工粗糙、細節全無；近處雜草斷茅之間立著一尊三十二吋高的石像，頸掛鏈環、腰繫圍裙；其後是石凳與一件石英淺皿——方形石塊，上面鑿出凹槽，下有環足承托，側面飾以蜥蜴：這些古石皿尚存籃編工藝的痕跡——由草編而木刻、終至石雕的演變一目了然。隔區立著伊德納本人的花崗石像，高三十六吋，厚唇闊鼻，左耳垂著一縷髮束——頭髮竟以細小的鐵釘插入小孔表現，鐵的這種用法在此屬首次得見。伊德納的「齒石」（獨石柱）前橫臥一條斷成四截的長石板，土人稱之為「伊德納的破盾」；末區的聖物園中，兩尊石英鱷像左右分立於水滴形聖石之前——其中一尊至今仍在一戶私宅中受人祭拜。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1910-12; the Idena complex of monoliths, quartz work and crocodile effigies, with Frobenius's craft-evolution reading reported as his interpretation.

passages.text: When, on leaving the main road, we arrive at the first small palm plantation, a group of quite coarse little pillars of stone about waist-high come into view; they are angular, roundish, and, at all events, roughly hewn or chipped off, absolutely bare of any detail. Going forward we come to another enclosure: here there is a wilderness of weeds, a mass of roof lattens and the straw of a collapsed thatch, amidst which rises a stone image about thirty-two inches high, roughly executed and defaced. It has one chain round its neck and another hangs over an apron skirt down to the hands folded over its stomach.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: Behind it I found the first of the stone-stools, and a dish made out of quartz: this, the first specimen of quartz work I had seen, was a four-square block whose upper surface had been chiselled to a depth of about one and a quarter inches, while the lower one had a raised ring on which it stood. All three stone-saucer specimens known to me were ornamented at the side with lizards. These ancient Ilifian stone saucers show indications of originally being basket work, developed in wood carving and transferred finally to sculpture in stone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the next enclosure was a stone statue of the Idena, a granite figure about thirty-six inches high above ground-level, exactly like the other figure with folded hands over the belly, aproned and ornately tasselled on its left; it has armlets, and a ruff-like ornament round its neck. The interesting part of the Idena is most decidedly its head, which had been knocked off and only insecurely replaced: the thick-lipped, broad-nosed face is negroid in type. A long lock or tassel of hair, missing on the right, hangs down from its left ear. The treatment of the hair in this granite head is especially of the very greatest interest: the hair is represented by little iron pegs, inserted in small holes. We here for the first time come upon this singular use of iron.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.

passages.text: In front of the Idena's tooth-stone or obelisk are the pieces of a long, narrow stone slab, fairly thin and of rough workmanship; it lies prone, broken in four pieces, with evidence of six or perhaps more holes having been bored into it at equal distances in its longitudinal axis. The natives call these particular fragments the broken buckler of the Idena. In a carelessly constructed hut at the fourth and last Idena enclosure, symmetrically placed, there is a stone crocodile to right and left in front of a stone block artificially rounded, set on end — drop-stones, varying but little in shape between a drop, an egg or an onion. One of the crocodiles made of quartz we dug up in Modeke; one, still worshipped in a private compound, is somewhat smaller.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Frobenius, The Voice of Africa, vol. I, ch. XIV (1913); not verbatim.
